title: 🎙️ REAL-TIME & VOICE
meta: This is a trigger file, not study material. Question visible → answer OUT LOUD → then expand → grade what you missed.
⭐ = decides the round. 🔥 = trending 2026. 📍 = you were asked this. 📝 = no vault note yet.

bands.name: The latency budget — the spine of every answer here

questions.text: What's the latency budget for a natural voice conversation?
points: Human turn-taking gaps are ~200–300 ms; past ~800 ms it reads as lag, past ~1.5 s people talk over it
Budget is a chain, not a number: capture + network + endpointing + STT final + LLM TTFT + TTS first-audio + playback
Endpointing is usually the biggest single slice — and it's a choice, not a constant
Every hop is additive, so the design question is always what can overlap
Quote shape, not invented figures: "sub-second end to end, with endpointing and LLM TTFT as the two levers"

links.label: latency in agentic systems
links.target: 03-Agentic-AI/11-Production Agentic Systems (architect lens)/93-latency in agentic systems

questions.flow: name the chain → find the two dominant slices → overlap what can overlap → budget per stage
questions.trap: answering with one total number and no per-stage breakdown

questions.text: Which latency does the user actually feel?
points: Time to first audio, not time to complete response — they hear the start, not the end
So: stream everything. First TTS chunk can play while the LLM is still generating
Perceived latency is also shaped: a filler/backchannel token buys real budget
Total duration matters for cost and for barge-in, not for the felt experience
Measure p95 first-audio per turn, not average end-to-end per session
questions.flow: first-audio is the felt metric → stream at every stage → shape perception → measure p95 per turn
questions.trap: optimising total response time while first-audio stays slow

questions.text: How do you overlap the stages instead of chaining them?
points: Streaming STT emits partials — start LLM prefill on a stable partial, don't wait for final
Speculative start: begin generating on the partial, discard if the final transcript diverges
Sentence/clause-boundary chunking into TTS → first audio before the LLM finishes
Prefetch and warm: TTS voice loaded, connections open, KV/prompt cache primed (07 #20)
Each overlap trades a little wasted compute for a lot of perceived latency
questions.flow: partial transcript → speculative prefill → clause-chunk to TTS → first audio early → discard on divergence
questions.trap: a strictly sequential STT→LLM→TTS pipeline, then blaming the models for latency

questions.text: What's the floor you can't optimise past?
points: Speed of light + routing: intercontinental RTT is tens to ~hundreds of ms and no engineering removes it
So region placement is a latency decision — media, inference and TTS should be co-located with the user
Audio framing adds inherent buffering (frame size, jitter buffer depth)
Provider cold starts and model load are avoidable floor — warm pools, not autoscale-from-zero
Say the floor out loud, then show what you optimise above it
questions.flow: RTT floor → co-locate media + inference → accept framing/jitter → keep pools warm
questions.trap: promising a latency target that violates the network floor for that geography

questions.text: Walk me through your voice pipeline end to end.
points: Capture → transport (WebRTC) → VAD/endpointing → streaming STT → LLM (+ tools/RAG) → TTS → playback
Two control loops running alongside: barge-in (#7) and turn state (who holds the floor)
Session state is per-call and stateful — this is not a stateless request/response service
Every stage streams; every stage needs its own timeout and fallback
Observability is per-turn: first-audio, endpoint delay, STT confidence, tokens, TTS latency
questions.flow: capture → transport → endpoint → STT → LLM → TTS → play, with barge-in and turn-state alongside
questions.trap: describing it as a request/response API — the state and the interrupt loops are the hard parts

questions.text: How do you know the user finished speaking?
points: VAD detects speech vs silence; endpointing decides the turn ended — related but not the same
Silence threshold is a direct latency↔interruption trade: short cuts people off mid-thought, long feels sluggish
Naive fixed silence is the weak answer. Better: semantic endpointing — is the utterance syntactically/semantically complete?
Adapt to context: expect a long pause after "my policy number is…", short after a yes/no question
Noise and accents break naive VAD — this is where real deployments fail
questions.flow: VAD detects speech → endpointer decides turn end → tune threshold as latency↔cutoff → semantic + context-aware beats fixed silence
questions.trap: treating endpointing as a constant rather than the biggest tunable slice of the budget

questions.text: The user talks while the agent is talking. What happens?
points: Barge-in: detect user speech during playback → stop TTS immediately, cancel the in-flight LLM call
Must cancel upstream too, or you pay for tokens nobody hears (01-PYTHON #31)
Then reconcile state: the agent said only part of its turn — the conversation history must record what was actually heard, not what was generated
Echo cancellation first, or the agent barges in on itself
Distinguish genuine interruption from backchannel ("mhm", "yeah") — cutting off on acknowledgement feels broken

links.label: streaming and real time agents
links.target: 03-Agentic-AI/11-Production Agentic Systems (architect lens)/99-streaming and real-time agents

questions.flow: detect speech during playback → kill TTS + cancel LLM → truncate history to what was heard → ignore backchannels
questions.trap: logging the full generated response into history when the user only heard four words of it

questions.text: Partial vs final transcripts — how do you use both?
points: Streaming STT emits unstable partials that get revised, then a stable final
Partials drive responsiveness: UI feedback, speculative prefill (#3), early intent detection
Only commit side effects on final — never fire a tool call off a partial
Confidence scores gate behaviour: low confidence → confirm rather than act
Domain vocabulary matters — boost/hint lists for names, drug names, policy numbers (#22)
questions.flow: partials for responsiveness → finals for commitment → confidence gates action → vocabulary hints for domain terms
questions.trap: triggering a tool or a transfer off a partial that later gets revised

questions.text: How do you stream text into speech?
points: Chunk on clause/sentence boundaries, not on token count — prosody needs a complete phrase
Too small → choppy, wrong intonation; too large → first-audio latency climbs
Keep an audio queue and play continuously; a gap mid-sentence is worse than a slightly later start
Numbers, dates, acronyms and units need normalisation before synthesis or they're read wrong
Cache synthesised audio for fixed phrases — greetings, disclaimers, hold messages
questions.flow: clause-boundary chunks → continuous playback queue → normalise text first → cache fixed phrases
questions.trap: chunking by fixed token count and getting flat or broken prosody

questions.text: Speech-to-speech models — do they replace your pipeline?
points: Native S2S removes the STT→LLM→TTS hops → much lower latency, preserves prosody, tone and emotion
Losses: no transcript checkpoint to inspect, weaker tool-calling and RAG integration in some stacks, less control per stage
Cascaded keeps debuggability, swappability and per-stage guardrails — you can see exactly where a turn went wrong
Regulated domains often require the transcript, which forces cascaded or a hybrid
Honest 2026 answer: hybrid — S2S for the conversational path, cascaded/tools for anything that acts
questions.flow: S2S wins latency and prosody → cascaded wins control, transcripts and tools → hybrid by path
questions.trap: presenting S2S as a pure upgrade with no loss of observability or control

questions.text: WebRTC or WebSocket for the audio?
points: WebRTC — UDP-based, built for media: jitter buffer, packet-loss concealment, echo cancellation, adaptive bitrate. Right for real user audio
WebSocket — TCP, simple, fine for server-to-server audio or where you control both ends and the network is good
TCP's head-of-line blocking is the killer for live audio — one lost packet stalls everything behind it
WebRTC costs complexity: signalling, ICE, STUN/TURN, more ops surface
Telephony path (SIP/PSTN) is a third option with its own codecs and constraints
questions.flow: real user audio over the internet → WebRTC · controlled server-to-server → WebSocket · TCP HOL blocking is why
questions.trap: WebSockets for browser mic audio, then debugging jitter you have no tools for

questions.text: Walk me through how a WebRTC call gets established.
points: Signalling (your channel, not WebRTC's): exchange SDP offer/answer describing media and codecs
ICE gathers candidates: host → STUN (discover public address, punch through NAT) → TURN (relay when direct fails)
Connectivity checks pick a candidate pair → DTLS handshake → SRTP media flows
TURN is the fallback that always works and always costs — it relays every byte
Renegotiation for changed tracks; ICE restart on network change (wifi → cellular)
questions.flow: signalling SDP → ICE candidates → STUN, then TURN if needed → DTLS → SRTP media
questions.trap: calling WebRTC peer-to-peer and forgetting that a real chunk of calls end up relayed

questions.text: TURN is expensive. What did you do about it?
points: TURN relays all media — it's bandwidth-priced and scales with concurrent minutes, not users
Cut the relay rate first: correct STUN setup, IPv6, host/srflx candidate hygiene, permissive-enough firewall guidance
Then cut cost per relayed minute: region-local TURN, self-hosted (coturn) vs managed, egress-aware placement
Capacity plan on concurrent relayed streams and bandwidth, not on registered users
Measure the relay ratio as a first-class metric — if it climbs, cost climbs linearly
questions.flow: measure relay ratio → reduce it via STUN/candidate hygiene → then region-local/self-hosted TURN → plan on concurrent bandwidth

questions.text: Network degrades mid-call. What does the user experience?
points: Jitter buffer absorbs variance — deeper buffer, smoother audio, more latency; it's the same trade again
Packet loss → concealment (PLC) fills gaps; beyond a few percent it's audible
Codec adapts bitrate (Opus) — degrade gracefully rather than dropping
Your pipeline must handle a degraded transcript, not just degraded audio: ASR confidence falls, so confirm more (#8, #20)
Have an explicit fallback: offer to switch to text/DTMF, or escalate to a human
questions.flow: jitter buffer absorbs variance → PLC covers loss → codec adapts → ASR confidence drops → confirm or escalate
questions.trap: designing only for the clean-network path

questions.text: A thousand concurrent calls. What breaks first?
points: Voice is stateful and long-lived — the whole stateless-autoscale playbook doesn't apply
Ceiling is usually concurrent sessions per instance (media + STT + TTS streams), not CPU or RPS
Scale on concurrency and drain, don't kill — a terminated pod drops live calls (02-FASTAPI #30)
Cold start is fatal here: keep warm pools, never scale from zero
Provider quotas — STT/TTS/LLM concurrency limits — bite before your own infra does
questions.flow: stateful sessions → scale on concurrency → warm pools, no cold start → drain on deploy → watch provider quotas
questions.trap: autoscaling on CPU/RPS and killing pods mid-call on every deploy

questions.text: Audio arrives faster than you can process it. Then what?
points: Audio is a real-time producer you cannot pause — the user keeps talking regardless
Bounded queue with an explicit overflow policy; unbounded means memory growth then OOM (01-PYTHON #31)
For live audio, dropping oldest usually beats blocking — stale audio is worthless, latency is everything
Detect the condition and degrade deliberately: smaller model, skip enrichment, shed non-critical work
Alert on queue depth — sustained backlog means you're under-provisioned, not momentarily unlucky
questions.flow: unpausable producer → bounded queue → drop stale over blocking → degrade deliberately → alert on depth

questions.text: Your STT provider degrades mid-call.
points: Per-stage timeout + circuit breaker; a stalled stage must not hang the turn
Fallback tiers: secondary provider · smaller/local model · degraded mode
Failover mid-call is the hard part — session state, audio buffer and stream handle must migrate or restart cleanly
Decide the honest failure UX: hold message, offer callback, escalate to human — silence is the worst outcome
Health-check providers continuously, not per call; break before the user notices
questions.flow: per-stage timeout → breaker → secondary provider or degraded mode → explicit spoken fallback, never silence
questions.trap: a fallback that requires restarting the call and loses the conversation

questions.text: What does a minute of conversation cost?
points: Stack the meters: STT per minute + LLM tokens per turn + TTS per character + TURN bandwidth + compute per session
Voice bills on time, not requests — an idle open call still costs
Token driver is history: every turn re-sends context, so cost grows within a call (06-AGENTIC-AI #22)
Levers: compact history (07 #16), smaller model for simple turns, cache fixed phrases (#9), cut relay ratio (#13)
Model p50 and p99 call cost — a long rambling call is the tail that hurts
questions.flow: per-minute STT/TTS + per-token LLM + relay bandwidth → cost grows within the call → compact, route, cache
questions.trap: pricing per request when the unit is a minute of open session

questions.text: How do you evaluate a voice agent?
points: Three layers, evaluated separately: ASR (WER, esp. on domain terms) · dialogue (task success, turns to completion) · audio (naturalness, prosody)
Plus real-time-specific metrics no text agent has: first-audio p95, endpoint delay, barge-in rate, talk-over rate, interruption recovery
Outcome metrics are what the business reads: containment/deflection, escalation rate, task completion
Replay recorded audio through the pipeline for regression — that's your test suite (06-AGENTIC-AI #20)
Synthetic audio only goes so far — real accents, noise and phone codecs are where it fails
questions.flow: ASR + dialogue + audio layers → plus first-audio/barge-in/talk-over → outcome metrics → replay real audio
questions.trap: quoting WER and stopping — it says nothing about whether the conversation worked

questions.text: ASR mishears a policy number. How does the system not act on it?
points: Errors propagate silently — the LLM receives a confident wrong string with no signal it's wrong
Use ASR confidence and n-best alternatives, not just the top hypothesis
Confirm high-stakes slots by reading back — IDs, amounts, names, dates. Cheap turn, huge error reduction
Constrain with domain knowledge: validate against a real format/checksum, or match against known values
Vocabulary boosting and phonetic matching for domain terms (#8) reduce the error at source
questions.flow: low confidence or high stakes → read back to confirm → validate against known formats → boost domain vocab
questions.trap: passing the top hypothesis straight into a tool call

questions.text: How does memory work when the conversation is live?
points: Two horizons: within-call (fast, complete, latency-critical) and across-call (retrieved, summarised)
Within-call history grows every turn and drives both latency and cost — compact it live (07 #16)
Anything retrieved mid-turn is on the critical path — pre-fetch on intent, or you blow the budget
Across-call memory must be written after the call, never on the hot path
Barge-in truncation (#7) must be reflected in memory or the agent "remembers" saying things nobody heard
questions.flow: within-call compacted live → retrieval pre-fetched off the critical path → cross-call written post-call
questions.trap: a synchronous vector search mid-turn that adds hundreds of ms to first-audio

questions.text: Design a hospital voice assistant — noise, privacy, latency, domain vocabulary.
points: Noise: near-field mic + echo cancellation, noise-robust ASR, confidence-gated confirmation (#20), graceful "I didn't catch that"
Privacy: PHI is the constraint — regional/on-prem inference, encryption in transit and at rest, redaction before logging, consent and recording rules, BAA-covered providers only
Latency: co-locate media + inference (#4), warm pools, streaming everywhere, semantic endpointing
Vocabulary: drug/procedure lexicon, vocabulary boosting, phonetic confusion handling, validate against a formulary
Safety: clinical actions are HITL — the agent captures and confirms, a human commits
questions.flow: noise → robust ASR + confirm · privacy → regional + redact + consent · latency → co-locate + stream · vocab → boosted lexicon · clinical → HITL
questions.trap: giving a generic voice-agent answer and never naming PHI, consent, or the clinical HITL boundary

questions.text: Multi-tenant real-time — what's different?
points: Noisy-neighbour is immediate and audible here — one tenant's spike degrades another's live call
Per-tenant concurrency caps, not just rate limits; reserve capacity for premium tiers
Isolation choice: shared pool (cheap, risky) → dedicated pools per tier → dedicated infra for regulated tenants
Per-tenant config is deep: voice, prompt, vocabulary, escalation rules, data-residency region
Every metric, log and trace tenant-tagged, or you can't attribute a degradation to anyone
questions.flow: concurrency caps per tenant → pool isolation by tier → per-tenant voice/vocab/region config → tenant-tagged telemetry
questions.trap: applying request-rate limiting to a workload whose unit is a concurrent session

questions.text: Do you record the call?
points: Consent is jurisdiction-dependent — two-party consent states, GDPR, sector rules; the disclosure itself is a design element
Separate the artifacts: raw audio · transcript · derived data. Each gets its own retention and access policy
Redact before persisting — PII/PHI stripped from logs and traces, not after the fact
Check provider terms: does your audio train their models? Zero-retention endpoints often exist and often must be requested
Right to erasure has to reach every copy: audio store, transcripts, vector index, memory store, backups

links.label: Privacy — memorization, PII extraction & data governance
links.target: 05-LLM-Production/11-Hallucination, Safety & Guardrails/07-Privacy — memorization, PII extraction & data governance

questions.flow: consent + disclosure → separate audio/transcript/derived retention → redact before write → zero-retention provider terms → erasure reaches every store
questions.trap: treating the vector index and memory store as exempt from deletion requests

questions.text: Tell me about the real-time system you built.
points: Open with the constraint, not the stack: "sub-second turn latency over consumer networks" beats "we used Deepgram and WebRTC"
The specific thing that broke — relay cost, backpressure, endpointing, barge-in state — and how you found it
The trade you made explicit: buffer depth vs latency, endpoint threshold vs cutting people off
What you rejected and why — the architect signal
Numbers: first-audio p95, relay ratio, cost per minute, dropped-frame rate. Any two, before → after
questions.flow: constraint → what broke → the trade you chose → what you rejected → two numbers
